title: Man who died after being hit with an Edmonton police taser was to appear in court
article: A man who died Monday after being hit with a city police Taser was to appear in court next week for a string of charges, including assaulting a peace officer causing bodily harm, show court records.
The man, identified by family as Marcel Moisan, would have celebrated his 50th birthday Thursday, Dec. 10.
Moisan was to appear in court Monday, Dec. 14, after Oct. 30 offences that led to charges of assault, two counts of obstructing a peace officer, and assaulting a peace officer causing bodily harm.

Moisan -- born Dec. 10, 1965 -- had last been in trouble with the law in March of 1998, when was handed six-months probation and had to enter a peace bond after being charged with assault and threatening injury or damage. In 1997, he was given 12 months probation for possession of a dangerous weapon (a bat).

Those who knew Moisan agree that while he had some sort of breakdown Monday, resulting in an 11:30 p.m. 911 call to police from the 12004 58 St. rental home where his wife and 14-year-old son also live, he should not have perished.
He was described by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), now probing the death, as agitated and carrying a knife when a Taser was deployed.
Moisan was under six feet tall and did not weigh more than 150 pounds, said one family friend who still can't comprehend the death.

"His wife and son were there, asking police not to shoot him. He was out of it and he dropped the knife after the Taser but he shouldn't have died," said a family friend, adding he hopes the ASIRT investigation doesn't take years.
Moisan went into medical distress after the Taser was used and was pronounced dead in hospital.
Despite Moisan's behaviour Monday night, family and friends agree on one thing, that he loved his wife and son, now left to cope with memories of his sudden and violent death just before Christmas.
One neighbour said the victim had just been over to her house giddy with excitement over a ring he had purchased for his wife for Christmas.

ASIRT's probe will focus on the circumstances surrounding the police contact with the victim to determine whether their conduct caused the death and, if so, whether that conduct constitutes a criminal offence. Cause of death will be determined by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner following an autopsy. This is the second in-custody Edmonton city police death since October and the third in 2015. The other two ASIRT cases have still not concluded.

* April 2012 -- Jeffrey Oatway, 34, is being held at city police headquarters when he is zapped with a Taser. After the Taser was used, officers noticed something serious was happening to Oatway's health and he had what police called a "medical episode." He had regained consciousness when he was taken to hospital, but died days later.

* Oct. 2008 -- Trevor Grimolfson, 38, dies after he was zapped three times by police with Tasers after storming through a Stony Plain Road pawnshop. The Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) ruled Grimolfson didn't die from the Taser -- it was the "very high levels" of ecstasy that led to his death by excited delirium.

* Dec. 2005 -- Alesandro Fiacco, 33, dies on the way to hospital after being zapped with a Taser by cops. Witnesses said he was behaving erratically and wandered into traffic near 113 Street and 76 Avenue. The medical examiner said he died of a cocaine overdose.

* March 2004 -- Ronald Perry, 25, dies after suffering a massive heart attack brought on by excited delirium. He was taken to hospital four days earlier following a struggle with cops that saw him jolted with a Taser.
